background_notes.fact: If a complex vector space has finite dimension n and an indexed family consists of n linearly independent vectors, that family is a basis.

grounds.reason: V has finite complex dimension λ+1.
The finite index set I has n elements and n>0.
Before the basis conclusion, the polynomial isolation argument proves linear independence of the e_i.

background_notes.justification: Choose a basis of n vectors, whose existence is part of finite dimension n, and express the given family as the columns of an n by n complex matrix. Independence says the homogeneous system has only the zero solution. Finite Gaussian elimination therefore has a pivot in every column and, since the matrix is square, every row. Thus every coordinate vector is a linear combination of the columns. The family spans and is independent, hence is a basis.

background_notes.fact: For integers m≥r≥0, m(m−1)⋯(m−r+1)/r!=binom(m,r) is an integer, with value 1 for r=0. Consequently the rising product (a+1)⋯(a+r)/r!=binom(a+r,r) is an integer for integers a,r≥0.

grounds.reason: λ is a nonnegative integer.
i∈I means i is an integer with 0≤i≤λ.
r is an arbitrary natural number in S004.
For the x branch take a=λ−i≥0; for the y branch take a=i≥0. The respective products are exactly these rising products.

background_notes.justification: On an m-element set the number of ordered r-tuples of distinct elements is m(m−1)⋯(m−r+1). Partition these tuples by their underlying r-element subset. Every class has r! elements, one for each ordering, so the quotient is the number of r-element subsets, the binomial coefficient. The empty tuple gives the r=0 case. Reversing the factors with m=a+r gives the rising-product identity.

background_notes.fact: If p is prime and 0≤j≤λ<p, then p does not divide binom(λ,j), and binom(λ,j) is a unit of R=Z_(p).
